title: Strange-metal behavior in correlated molecular conductors
authors: Savita Priya, Maxim Wenzel, Christian Prange, Bertold Rasche, Christian Sindlinger, Takuya Kobayashi, Hiromi Taniguchi, Dita Puspita Sari, Yasuyuki Ishii, Kazuya Miyagawa, Kazushi Kanoda, Simone Fratini, Martin Dressel
abstract: The $κ$-BEDT-TTF salts are prototypical Mott systems, realizing a correlation-driven electronic transition from a Fermi-liquid state to a Mott insulator. The metallic compounds with spatially modulated Hg-containing anions, $κ$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4$Hg$_{3-δ}X_8$ ($X$ = Br, and Cl), however, fall outside this classification. Our temperature-dependent transport and broad-range optical investigations reveal a $ρ(T)\propto T$ dependence of the resistivity up to elevated temperatures and a power-law behavior of the frequency-dependent conductivity $\vert\hatσ (ω)\vert \propto ω^{-0.7}$; well-known hallmarks of ``strange metals''. The linear-in-frequency scattering rate of these strange metals scales to the Planckian dissipation. We demonstrate that this response only occurs in systems with incommensurate anion layers and establish a direct link to large-scale spatial modulations. Our conclusions can be extended to other strongly correlated strange-metal compounds
summary: This work characterizes the 'strange-metal' state in $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4	ext{Hg}_{3-\delta}	ext{X}_8$ by showing linear temperature dependence of resistivity and $\omega^{-0.7}$ optical response. The authors argue that this anomalous behavior, marked by Planckian dissipation, arises specifically due to large-scale spatial modulations within the anion layers, distinguishing it from standard Fermi liquid behavior.
main_problem: The paper investigates the origin of 'strange-metal' behavior in molecular conductors, characterized by charge transport that violates conventional metal power laws.
main_result: The strange metal behavior in $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4	ext{Hg}_{3-\delta}	ext{X}_8$ is linked to the presence of incommensurate anion layers and large-scale spatial modulations, leading to Planckian dissipation scaling.
method: The study combines temperature-dependent transport measurements ($ho(T)$) with broad-range optical investigations using frequency-dependent complex conductivity ($\hat{\sigma}(\omega)$).
model_or_system: The physical system is $\kappa$-BEDT-TTF salts, comparing $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4	ext{Hg}_{3-\delta}	ext{X}_8$ (strange metal candidate) against $\kappa$-CuBr and $\kappa$-CuNCS (Fermi liquid reference).
key_observables: Resistivity ($ho(T) \propto T$ vs $T^2$), frequency-dependent conductivity ($|\hat{\sigma}(\omega)| \propto \omega^{-0.7}$ vs $\omega^{-1}$), and the frequency dependence of the scattering rate ($\Gamma(\omega) \propto \omega$ vs $\omega^2$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), frequency ($\omega$), and the ratio $\hbar\Gamma/k_B T \approx 1.2$ (Planckian dissipation).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing the observed spectral weight transfer and scattering rate scaling against established theoretical expectations for Fermi liquids.
figures_summary: Figures compare $ho(T)$ and $\Gamma(\omega)$ for strange metals vs. Fermi liquids, showing the characteristic linear ($\omega$) vs. quadratic ($\omega^2$) scaling of the scattering rate.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the electronic signatures of strange metals ($\kappa$-Hg$_3-\delta$X$_8$) against conventional Fermi liquids ($\kappa$-CuBr, $\kappa$-CuNCS) using transport and optical measurements to pinpoint the role of structural modulation.
why_interesting: The direct link established between structural disorder (incommensurate anion layers) and the emergence of Planckian dissipation scaling in transport properties is highly relevant to understanding non-Fermi liquid physics in correlated materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Crystal structure of κ-(BEDT-TTF)4Hg3−δX8, composed of conducting BEDT-TTF layers separated by insulating anion layers. (b) Incommensurate Hg-X anion layer in κ-Hg3−δX8 viewed from a different angle. (c) Temperature-dependent dc resistivity of the strange metals, demonstrating ρ(T) ∝T; and (d) electrical resistivity vs. T 2 plot for two correlated Fermi liquids, revealing the ρ(T) ∝T 2 response. The red dashed lines are guides to the eye.

FIG. 2. Absolute value of the complex conductivity as a function of frequency, |ˆσ(ω)|, obtained at various temperatures as indicated. The free carrier response is observed predominantly up to 150 meV (1200 cm−1), above which the electronic response is affected by Hubbard band and interband transitions, along with sharp molecular vibrations coupled to the electronic response. The Drude-type ω−1 decay is observed for the Fermi-liquid metals (a) κ-CuBr and (b) κ-CuNCS when low temperatures are approached. For the strange metals (c) κ-Hg3−δBr8 and (d) κ-Hg3−δCl8, the itinerant carriers follow a power-law |ˆσ(ω)| ∝ω−0.7, which is much flatter than that observed in the Fermi liquid compounds....

FIG. 3. Frequency-dependent scattering rates extracted for different temperatures in the metallic states. The upper panels display Γ(ω) on a linear energy scale. The lower panels illustrate that the canonical metals (a,b) κ-CuBr and (c,d) κ-CuNCS approach a Γ(ω) ∝ω2 behavior at 10 K expected for a Fermi-liquid response. In the case of the strange metals (e) κ-Hg3−δBr8 and (g) κ-Hg3−δCl8, the scattering rate increases linearly with frequency: Γ(ω) ∝ω (the dashed lines are guides to the eye). Following the idea of Planckian scattering limit, in the two lower-row panels (f,h) the axes are scaled by the respective temperature. In a wide range, the data collapse to single curves.
